Intermolecular interactions and structural evolution of candidate soy protein isolate/xylitol adhesives under heat treatment and tannic acid modulation
Effects of different packaging materials on the frozen storage quality of strawberries: A study based on functional active components and aroma
Camel–plant protein blends modulate protein digestibility and peptidomic profiles under simulated infant gastrointestinal conditions (part I)
abstract: Blending animal and plant proteins can offer sustainability benefits in infant formula production, yet the digestion dynamics of such mixed-protein matrices during infancy remains largely unexplored. This study investigated the digestion behaviour of camel milk, chickpea and oat proteins and their blends using a static in vitro gastrointestinal digestion model representative of 6–12-month-old infants. Proteolysis, structural disintegration and peptide profiling were examined and the results demonstrated that camel–chickpea blend exhibited synergistic digestion, characterized by relatively higher amino acid and peptide release. In contrast, antagonistic aggregation in the camel–oat blend restricted enzyme access and obstructed proteolysis. Moreover, blend-specific peptides, that were not generated in the corresponding single-source proteins, were detected across all blends. These findings demonstrate that protein compatibility governs the digestive restructuring of the protein matrix during infant digestion and identify camel–chickpea blend as a potentially highly digestible and amino acid-sufficient base for infant formulations.

title: Insights into corn phenolamides: chemical profiling, quantification in whole-grain corn products, and thermal effects
abstract: Corn (maize; Zea mays L.) is a staple food for over one billion people and a source of phenolamides, an under-characterized class of phytochemicals relevant to bioactivity and processing-driven sensory traits. We mapped the phenolamide chemical space of whole-grain corn products using UHPLC-HRMS/MS coupled with Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking (GNPS) and targeted MS/MS annotation. Twenty-eight phenolamides spanning seven amine-conjugate subclasses (putrescine, cadaverine, spermidine, spermine, tyramine, tryptamine, and serotonin) were annotated based on their MS/MS fragmentation patterns in positive ion mode. Characteristic neutral losses of 137, 160, and 176 Da supported the annotation of tyramine-, tryptamine-, and serotonin-derived conjugates, respectively. Notably, this study represents the first report of feruloyl tyramine and feruloyl serotonin in whole grains and provides evidence for a putative reduced analog of the macrocyclic spermine conjugate chaenorpine, tentatively assigned as dihydrochaenorpine. Major phenolamides were synthesized, structurally confirmed by MS/MS and NMR, and used to develop a LC-MS quantification workflow applied to commercial products (corn grits, cornmeal, popcorn, frozen corn, and freeze-dried corn). Nineteen phenolamides were quantified. Di- p -coumaroyl spermidine (diCouSpd), chaenorpine, and diferuloyl putrescine (diFerPut) were dominant constituents. Chaenorpine was most abundant in corn grits (34.91–151.22 mg/100 g), while diCouSpd and related spermidine phenolamides were highest in popcorns (92.23–327.36 mg/100 g). Both classes occurred at trace or negligible levels in frozen and freeze-dried corn, likely reflecting sweet-corn varietal origin. Putrescine-derived phenolamides were also elevated in popcorns (9.57–34.29 mg/100 g) and lower levels in frozen and freeze-dried products. Thermal experiments showed transient increases under moderate heating and popping, whereas severe/prolonged heating caused compound-class-dependent losses, particularly among spermidine/spermine conjugates. These findings expand the phenolamide diversity of whole-grain corn and provide a processing-relevant framework for optimizing retention of bioactive phenolamides in corn products.

title: Nanosecond pulsed electric field (nsPEF) processing better preserves donor human milk digestibility than holder pasteurisation during dynamic in vitro term infant digestion
abstract: This study compared the digestibility of nanosecond pulsed electric field (nsPEF)-treated donor human milk (DHM) to raw (RHM) and Holder pasteurised (HoP-HM) samples using a dynamic in vitro digestion model simulating term infant conditions. Structural analysis showed that HoP-HM formed larger fat-protein aggregates throughout digestion, likely due to heat-induced protein aggregation. Proteolysis was significantly higher ( p < 0.05) in PEF-HM, particularly at the start of the gastric phase and at the end of the intestinal phase. SDS-PAGE showed stronger intact lactoferrin bands in PEF-HM than in HoP-HM. Targeted lipidomic analysis (570 species) identified treatment-related differences at the start of digestion that diminished as digestion progressed. Similarly, most analysed fatty acid levels were initially higher in PEF-HM but diminished afterwards. Overall, nsPEF showed a digestion profile closer to RHM than HoP-HM, supporting further evaluation of nsPEF as a candidate non-thermal processing technology. However, these in vitro findings require in vivo validation.

β-Mannanases from Flavobacterium saccharophilum produce β-mannooligosaccharides with prebiotic potential
Improving the quality of gluten-free rice dough and bread: The role and mechanism of native and ultrasonically treated pea protein
Effects of feeding apple and hempseed by-products on fatty acids, B vitamins and mineral concentrations of dairy cow milk
Co-exposure to bisphenols promotes the uptake of nanoplastics by colon cancer cells: mechanisms and implications
LC-HRMS-based target, suspect and non-target screening of Greek peaches and nectarines: pesticide occurrence, transformation products and dietary risk assessment
abstract: Peaches and nectarines ( Prunus persica ) are widely consumed stone fruits requiring comprehensive residue monitoring. Herein, an integrated LC-HRMS workflow combining target, suspect, and non-target screening was applied to 74 samples collected from the two major Greek production subregions. Target analysis enabled the quantification of 22 pesticide residues with cyprodinil, tebuconazole, difenoconazole, boscalid, fludioxonil, etofenprox, and pyraclostrobin among the most frequently detected. Comparison with EU MRLs showed only two slight exceedances, corresponding to 2.7% of samples, below the recent EFSA-reported average. Target-driven suspect screening, supported by literature-derived MS data, retention time prediction, and in silico MS/MS fragmentation, enabled the tentative annotation of nine transformation products associated with five pesticides. Non-target screening expanded chemical characterization by annotating emerging contaminants and endogenous compounds. Dietary risk assessment indicated acute and chronic exposure below toxicological reference values, suggesting no appreciable consumer risk. The workflow demonstrates the value of integrated LC-HRMS for pesticide monitoring and broader chemical profiling.
